objectAssessments.assessment: Fixed amount, unchanged composition, fixed volume and ideal-gas scope are stated before deriving pressure from the state equation. Charles, French and 1787 retain this object's ownership. Broader wording avoids claiming the historical experiment established the isochoric result. Theory explicitly does not replace real-gas/apparatus experiments; this is the same narrative scientific clarification as the Chinese comparator, not an altered source formula.

Footnote marker and 1787 are retained. Charles precedes Gay-Lussac and did not then publish. The relation is explicitly volume versus temperature at constant pressure, separate from the lesson's pressure relation at constant volume. No historical relation is harmonized to the title.
Equation (2-19) gives p=(mR/(mu V))T, still numbered (2-20). Both denominator factors remain. Fixed mass, composition and volume keep its coefficient constant. No symbol or number changes.

The law statement specifies ideal gas, fixed mass/composition/volume, absolute pressure and absolute temperature. The body explicitly follows the original textbook's Charles's law naming. The separate kelvin paragraph excludes directly using Celsius numerical readings; it does not convert the title to a modern alternate name.

The same ideal-gas sample in equal-volume equilibrium states has p1/p2=T1/T2, still equation (2-21). These are absolute pressures, not pressure differences from surrounding air. The prior kelvin restriction remains applicable and no gauge-pressure ratio or Celsius-temperature ratio is licensed.

Empty source-bound fig-25 placeholder and original position remain. The display label is localized to Figure 25; source.data retains the original Chinese label. No new figure, numerical data or written task is introduced.

The cross-page paragraph closes in order. Isochoric process is defined as constant volume with pressure/temperature changing; isochore is defined as the straight p-T graph line. Axes are absolute T horizontally and absolute p vertically. For the same amount/composition at equal positive T, V1<V2 gives higher pressure and steeper slope for V1. It is not a comparison of different gas amounts or an isobaric process.
Separate Figure 25 caption and source ownership/placement remain. It adds no new measured value or science claim.

Correctly separates two model limits: fixed positive volume gives pressure tending to zero, whereas fixed nonzero pressure gives volume tending to zero. Fixed volume does not also vanish. The origin is an ideal-model extrapolation; possible liquefaction prevents treating it as an uninterrupted real-gas trajectory. All qualifications survive actual flow. However, extrapolation is repeated without a plain definition and liquefy is unglossed at this essential model-versus-real-gas distinction.
The first original proof request remains prose: prove p=p0 gamma T, equation (2-22), with gas mass/composition/volume unchanged. No worked answer or exercise object has been added.

p0 is the same sample's pressure at the same fixed volume at source T=273 K, not an atmospheric/gauge reference or an arbitrary starting pressure. Gamma is named the pressure-temperature coefficient. Equality with the corresponding volume-expansion coefficient is explicitly inside the source integer-reference approximation, not a claim that 273 K is an exact modern Celsius-zero definition.

The source Greek gamma, approximation sign, fraction 1/273, equality to alpha and inverse-temperature-interval unit are preserved. Kelvin wording localizes the original unit outside math. The reciprocal is not taken of an arbitrary Celsius numerical reading.

The coefficient is explained as pressure increase for a one-degree temperature interval at fixed volume divided by the specified reference pressure. Equal-sized Celsius/kelvin intervals do not imply equal absolute readings. The denominator is not replaced by pressure at an arbitrary initial temperature.

The second original prose request still derives two separate laws from Mendeleev-Clapeyron (2-19), keeping amount/composition fixed: fixed T for Boyle-Mariotte (2-2), separately fixed p for Gay-Lussac (2-7). All compound historical identities and item-specific source_term/reason declarations remain. No new task, supplied answer or combined simultaneous-fixed-T-and-p derivation is invented.

independentScienceReasoning.scope: Reviewer reasoning only; these derivations were not inserted into the learner draft and do not solve or replace its retained prose prompts.
independentScienceReasoning.fixedVolumeRatio: For the same gas sample C=mR/(mu V) is constant and p=C T. Thus p1/p2=T1/T2 uses absolute pressures and kelvin temperatures, provided the denominator state has nonzero absolute T/p. Adding/subtracting atmospheric pressure or a Celsius offset does not preserve this ratio.
independentScienceReasoning.isochoreOrdering: At fixed gas amount/composition the p-T slope is mR/(mu V). Increasing the fixed positive volume lowers that slope. Therefore V1<V2 places V1 above V2 at any shared positive T; the two lines share only the ideal extrapolated zero.
independentScienceReasoning.constrainedLimits: With V fixed and positive, p approaches zero as T approaches zero. With p fixed and nonzero, V approaches zero instead. These are different constraints, not simultaneous disappearance of fixed volume and pressure. A real gas may leave the gaseous phase before that extension reaches zero.
independentScienceReasoning.coefficient: With T0=273 K as the source integer reference, p0=C T0 and gamma=1/T0. A one-kelvin pressure increment divided by p0 is 1/273; equal-sized Celsius and kelvin intervals support the same interval coefficient, not a reciprocal-Celsius-reading interpretation. The source approximation and alpha relation are unchanged.
independentScienceReasoning.separateDerivations: For fixed amount/composition, pV/T is constant. Holding T fixed gives the Boyle-Mariotte relation. Holding absolute p fixed separately gives the source's Gay-Lussac V/T relation. Neither is obtained by holding volume fixed; names are kept according to the source.

quotes: Extrapolating these straight isochores takes them through the origin $O$.
A real gas can liquefy at low temperature;
findings.problem: At the essential boundary between a mathematical extension and a real-gas state, the child is expected to infer what extrapolating and liquefy mean. Repeating ideal-gas model extrapolation does not explain the operation. The no-real-continuous-origin qualification is scientifically correct but less usable without explaining that the gas can become liquid.
findings.requestedRevision: Within this same prose object, explain extrapolation as extending the straight lines toward lower temperatures, and gloss liquefy as turn into a liquid. Split the long fixed-volume limit sentence if necessary while retaining both separate constraints, the origin O, the nonzero-pressure condition and the real-gas qualification. Do not add a new lesson object, exercise, worked solution, numerical measurement or figure edit.
findings.suggestedOpening: Extending these straight isochores toward lower temperatures is called extrapolation. The extended lines pass through the origin $O$.
findings.suggestedRealGasSentence: A real gas can liquefy, meaning turn into a liquid, at low temperature.
